cards.front: What is the SVD of an m×n matrix A?
cards.back: A = U Σ V^T where U (m×m) and V (n×n) are orthogonal, Σ (m×n) is diagonal with entries σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … ≥ σᵣ > 0 (singular values) and the rest zero; r = rank(A).

cards.front: How are the singular values σ_i related to the eigenvalues of AᵀA?
cards.back: AᵀA is symmetric positive semidefinite; its eigenvalues satisfy λ_i = σ_i² ≥ 0. Thus σ_i = √λ_i (ordered decreasingly).

cards.front: Derive the right singular vectors V from AᵀA.
cards.back: By the spectral theorem, AᵀA v_i = λ_i v_i yields an orthonormal basis {v_i} of ℝⁿ. Set V = [v_1 … v_n]; the first r vectors correspond to λ_i > 0.

cards.front: How are the left singular vectors u_i (i=1..r) obtained?
cards.back: For each σ_i > 0 define u_i = (1/σ_i) A v_i. Then ||u_i||=1 and u_iᵀ u_j = δ_{ij} because v_i are orthonormal eigenvectors of AᵀA.

cards.front: How is the orthonormal basis for U completed when r < m?
cards.back: The remaining m-r vectors are chosen as an orthonormal basis for ker(AAᵀ), i.e., eigenvectors of AAᵀ belonging to eigenvalue 0; they are orthogonal to the first r vectors.

cards.front: Why does every real matrix possess an SVD?
cards.back: AᵀA always admits a spectral decomposition (symmetric). The construction above produces orthogonal U, V and diagonal Σ satisfying A = U Σ Vᵀ.

cards.front: State the ordering and multiplicity properties of singular values.
cards.back: σ₁ ≥ … ≥ σₙ ≥ 0; the number of strictly positive σ_i equals rank(A); each σ_i has multiplicity equal to the geometric multiplicity of λ_i = σ_i² in AᵀA.
